In one sentence: an animal service role that provides feeding, cleaning, observation, grooming and exercise care for non-food animals such as dogs and cats, keeps honest records of animal condition, and communicates with pet owners and visitors.

The work of Animal Care and Service Workers falls into four categories: daily care (feeding and watering according to schedules and instructions; washing facility linens and cleaning, tidying, maintaining and disinfecting animal housing and equipment such as saddles and halters; regulating temperature and humidity in housing, nursery rooms and exhibit areas; exercising animals); health observation and assisted handling (examining and observing animals to detect signs of illness, disease or injury; mixing food, liquid formulas, medications and supplements according to instructions, prescriptions and species knowledge; providing treatment for sick or injured animals or contacting a veterinarian to obtain treatment; anesthetizing and vaccinating animals according to instructions; cleaning and disinfecting surgical equipment); grooming and customer service (performing grooming work such as bathing, brushing, clipping and trimming coats, trimming nails and cleaning ears; discussing pets' grooming needs with clients; advising pet owners on pet health care; answering visitors' questions about animal behaviour, habitats and breeding habits; answering the telephone and scheduling appointments; selling pet food and supplies; teaching children to feed and care for animals); and records, adoption and facilities (collecting and recording weight, body size, body condition, treatments, medications and food intake; finding adoptive homes for stray or abandoned animals; moving animals between enclosures; installing, maintaining and repairing equipment such as infrared lamps, feeding devices and cages; ordering, unloading and storing feed and supplies; diving to maintain exhibit areas in aquariums; training animals; training volunteers and facility staff). These are the U.S. task scope; actual diagnosis and treatment in China is checked separately against qualifications, filing and institutional licensing, and does not grant ordinary care staff independent operating authority. Record requirements: ordinary animal care, adoption and customer records are kept honestly under the applicable rules, original values may be retained and corrected in line with the standards; medical records at animal diagnosis and treatment institutions have a separate statutory retention requirement of at least three years, and ordinary care records are not all subject to the same period.

values: Fictional materials and rules

A: You are a paper learner with no on-site or diagnostic and treatment authorization. In the original table at 9:30, D1 was given 120 g, 30 g remained and 90 g was consumed, and behaviour was recorded as not observed; D2 was given 100 g and the amount remaining is blank. The numbers are a fictional calculation only and have no species nutrition or safety meaning.

B: The handover at 9:35 refers to the same 9:30 original table, recording the intake for D1 as 80 g and behaviour as normal. No recipient, reviewer or feedback was given.

C: Paper intake equals the amount given minus the amount remaining, with missing figures to be checked; compare the same identifier, time point and fields, retain both original values, and report the difference and the unknown to the trainer; do not infer animal health, invent feedback or carry out feeding, diagnosis and treatment or grooming.
Three paper tasks

Task 1: list the two intake calculations for D1/D2 and the original table and handover values, marking missing figures as to be checked.
Task 2: check the intake and behaviour fields of the same 9:30 record for D1 and write the difference and who it is reported to.
Task 3: write three sentences covering the fact, the unknown and the next communication step, and do not claim that the handover has been corrected or that the animal's health is normal.
Reference deliverable

Reference 1: D1 = 120−30 = 90 g; the amount remaining for D2 is not given, so the intake is to be checked and 0 is not filled in.
Reference 2: the original table for D1 is 90 g / not observed and the handover is 80 g / normal, referring to the same 9:30 record; the two fields conflict, so retain the original values and report to the trainer.

Reference 3: it can be said that discrepancies in two fields have been found; the intake for D2 and the recipient and feedback are unknown; ask the trainer to check the original record and the basis for the handover, and do not invent a reply or correction or a diagnosis.
Practice verification boundaries

Only paper data, calculations and communication are verified; feeding amounts, nutrition, animal health and operational safety are not verified, and no animal handling is carried out.
The four pieces follow A/B/C: the two calculations, the two-field difference, the three-sentence communication and the review of authority; they do not represent a skill level, independent care or a diagnostic and treatment licence.

The work involves feeding and cleaning, observation and record-keeping, grooming, exercise and customer service for non-food animals such as dogs and cats, in settings that include kennels, shelters, zoos and aquariums.
